intro:
השבוע נשאל את השאלה שכל חוקר שואל בסוף: איזה מודל הכי טוב? נחזור לנתוני מחלת הלב משבוע 9, ונשווה שלושה מסווגים: רגרסיה לוגיסטית, KNN, ו-Random Forest — מודל שמבוסס על „חוכמת ההמונים״ של הרבה עצי החלטה.

נלמד להשוות בצורה הוגנת: אותו סט אימון, אותו סט בדיקה, ואותם מדדים — דיוק, רגישות, סגוליות ו-AUC. ונשאל גם שאלה שאינה סטטיסטית: מה יקר יותר, לפספס חולה או להתריע לשווא?

זה השבוע שבו כל מה שלמדנו מתחבר: טבלאות, לולאות, פונקציות, גרפים ומודלים.

hw.title: המטלה השבועית (שבוע 11)
context: נחזור לקובץ מחלת הלב משבוע 9 (heart.csv): age (גיל), sex (מין), restbps (לחץ דם במנוחה), chol (כולסטרול), bs (רמת סוכר בדם), maxhr (דופק מרבי), ו-target (האם אירע לנבדק אירוע לבבי, 0/1). המטרה: להשוות שלושה מודלים שמסווגים מי עבר אירוע לבבי.
lines: 1. טענו את הקובץ, הציגו את מימדיו ואת מספר הנבדקים בכל ערך של target.
1. בדקו כמה מהשורות בקובץ הן כפילויות של נבדק אחר (שורות זהות בכל העמודות מלבד bs). הסירו את הכפילויות (השאירו מכל נבדק שורה אחת) והדפיסו כמה נבדקים נשארו.
1. כתבו בהערה בקוד: מה היה קורה להערכת המודלים אם אותו נבדק היה מופיע גם בסט האימון וגם בסט הבדיקה? (המושג: דליפת מידע, data leakage)
1. קבעו זרע אקראי (seed) כדי שהתוצאות יהיו שחזוריות, וחלקו את הנתונים לסט אימון (70%) וסט בדיקה (30%).
1. תקננו את המשתנים המנבאים לפי הממוצע וסטיית התקן של סט האימון בלבד. כתבו בהערה בקוד: למה לא משתמשים בסט הבדיקה לתקנון?
1. התאימו רגרסיה לוגיסטית על סט האימון, וחשבו את ההסתברויות החזויות לסט הבדיקה.
1. התאימו מודל KNN עם K=15, וחשבו את הסיווג החזוי לסט הבדיקה.
1. התאימו מודל Random Forest עם 500 עצים, וחשבו את הסיווג החזוי ואת ההסתברויות החזויות לסט הבדיקה.
1. לכל מודל הדפיסו confusion matrix, וחשבו דיוק (accuracy), רגישות (sensitivity) וסגוליות (specificity), לפי סף של 0.5.
1. כתבו פונקציה שמקבלת את הערכים האמיתיים ואת הסיווג החזוי ומחזירה את שלושת המדדים — והשתמשו בה לכל שלושת המודלים.
1. ארגנו את המדדים בטבלה אחת (data frame) שבה כל שורה היא מודל וכל עמודה היא מדד, והדפיסו אותה.
1. צרו גרף עמודות שמשווה את הדיוק של שלושת המודלים.
1. כתבו בהערה בקוד: איזה מודל עדיף לדעתכם, ומה עוד הייתם רוצים לדעת לפני שמחליטים (רמז: מה יקר יותר — לפספס חולה, או להתריע לשווא?)
1. חשבו AUC לרגרסיה הלוגיסטית ול-Random Forest, וציירו את שתי עקומות ה-ROC על אותו גרף.
1. חזרו על כל התהליך עם 5 זרעים אקראיים שונים (בלולאה), והציגו את הדיוק הממוצע של כל מודל. מה זה מלמד על היציבות של ההשוואה?

כותרות הקוד: השתמשו בפורמט הכותרות של הקורס, וכתבו בתחילת הקובץ את שם הקורס, השבוע, מספר תעודת הזהות שלכם ושמכם.

# Foundations of programming for empirical science
# Week 11
# assignment by < First Name > < Last Name >, id < 123456789 >

library(ggplot2)
library(class)
library(randomForest)


#### DATA PREPARATION ####

# 1. Load the data, dimensions, subjects per target value
df = read.csv("heart.csv")
dim(df)
table(df$target)

# 2. Remove duplicated patients: rows identical on all columns except bs
same_patient = duplicated(df[, c("age", "sex", "restbps", "chol", "maxhr", "target")])
sum(same_patient)
df = df[!same_patient, ]
nrow(df)

# 3. Data leakage: if the same patient is in both the training and the test set,
# the model is tested on subjects it has already seen (and can memorize). The
# test accuracy is then too optimistic and does not reflect new patients.

# 4. Seed and 70/30 split
set.seed(42)
n           = nrow(df)
train_index = sample(1:n, size = round(0.7 * n))

df_train = df[train_index, ]
df_test  = df[-train_index, ]

# 5. Standardize the predictors by the mean and sd of the training set only
# Why not the test set: the test set stands for new subjects the model has never
# seen. Using its mean and sd leaks information from the test set into the model,
# and makes the evaluation too optimistic.
predictors = c("age", "sex", "restbps", "chol", "bs", "maxhr")
train_mean = colMeans(df_train[, predictors])
train_sd   = apply(df_train[, predictors], 2, sd)

x_train = scale(df_train[, predictors], center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
x_test  = scale(df_test[, predictors],  center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
y_train = df_train$target
y_test  = df_test$target


#### THREE MODELS ####

# 1. Logistic regression: predicted probabilities for the test set
train_s     = data.frame(x_train, target = y_train)
logit_model = glm(target ~ ., data = train_s, family = binomial)
logit_prob  = predict(logit_model, newdata = data.frame(x_test), type = "response")
logit_class = ifelse(logit_prob >= 0.5, 1, 0)

# 2. KNN with K = 15: predicted class for the test set
knn_class = knn(train = x_train, test = x_test, cl = y_train, k = 15)
knn_class = as.numeric(as.character(knn_class))

# 3. Random forest with 500 trees: predicted probabilities and class
rf_model = randomForest(x = x_train, y = as.factor(y_train), ntree = 500)
rf_prob  = predict(rf_model, x_test, type = "prob")[, "1"]
rf_class = ifelse(rf_prob >= 0.5, 1, 0)


#### COMPARE PERFORMANCE ####

# 1. Confusion matrix for each model
table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = logit_class)
table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = knn_class)
table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = rf_class)

# 2. A function that returns accuracy, sensitivity and specificity
get_metrics = function(actual, predicted) {
  accuracy    = mean(predicted == actual)
  sensitivity = sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 1) / sum(actual == 1)
  specificity = sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 0) / sum(actual == 0)
  return(c(accuracy = accuracy, sensitivity = sensitivity, specificity = specificity))
}

# 3. One table: a row per model, a column per metric
results = data.frame(
  model = c("Logistic regression", "KNN (K = 15)", "Random forest"),
  rbind(get_metrics(y_test, logit_class),
        get_metrics(y_test, knn_class),
        get_metrics(y_test, rf_class))
)
print(results)

# 4. Bar plot of the accuracy of the three models
ggplot(results, aes(x = model, y = accuracy)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Test accuracy by model", x = "Model", y = "Accuracy")

# 5. Which model is better?
# After removing the duplicated patients the three models are close (about 0.7
# accuracy), and with only ~90 test patients the differences are small. Logistic
# regression is the simplest and about as good as the others, so I would prefer it.
# Before deciding we would want to know the cost of each error: missing a sick
# patient (low sensitivity) is usually worse than a false alarm, so we may prefer
# the model with the best sensitivity, or lower the 0.5 threshold. We would also
# check that the differences are stable across other splits of the data (see bonus).


#### BONUS ####

library(pROC)

# 1. AUC and ROC curves for logistic regression and random forest
roc_logit = roc(y_test, logit_prob)
roc_rf    = roc(y_test, rf_prob)
auc(roc_logit)
auc(roc_rf)

plot(roc_logit, col = "blue", legacy.axes = TRUE, main = "ROC curves - test set",
     xlab = "False Positive Rate", ylab = "True Positive Rate")
plot(roc_rf, col = "red", add = TRUE)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Logistic regression", "Random forest"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2)

# 2. Repeat the whole process with 5 seeds and average the accuracy
seeds    = 1:5
accuracy = data.frame()

for (s in seeds) {
  set.seed(s)
  train_index = sample(1:n, size = round(0.7 * n))
  df_train    = df[train_index, ]
  df_test     = df[-train_index, ]

  train_mean = colMeans(df_train[, predictors])
  train_sd   = apply(df_train[, predictors], 2, sd)
  x_train    = scale(df_train[, predictors], center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
  x_test     = scale(df_test[, predictors],  center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
  y_train    = df_train$target
  y_test     = df_test$target

  logit_model = glm(target ~ ., data = data.frame(x_train, target = y_train), family = binomial)
  logit_class = ifelse(predict(logit_model, data.frame(x_test), type = "response") >= 0.5, 1, 0)
  knn_class   = as.numeric(as.character(knn(x_train, x_test, cl = y_train, k = 15)))
  rf_model    = randomForest(x = x_train, y = as.factor(y_train), ntree = 500)
  rf_class    = ifelse(predict(rf_model, x_test, type = "prob")[, "1"] >= 0.5, 1, 0)

  accuracy = rbind(accuracy, data.frame(
    seed     = s,
    logistic = mean(logit_class == y_test),
    knn      = mean(knn_class == y_test),
    rf       = mean(rf_class == y_test)
  ))
}

print(accuracy)
colMeans(accuracy[, c("logistic", "knn", "rf")])
# The accuracy of each model changes by several points from seed to seed, and so
# does the ranking of the models. One split of ~300 patients is not enough to pick
# a winner; the average over seeds is more trustworthy (logistic regression is
# slightly ahead), but the models are close.

# Foundations of programming for empirical science
# Week 11
# assignment by < First Name > < Last Name >, id < 123456789 >

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, roc_curve, roc_auc_score


#### DATA PREPARATION ####

# 1. Load the data, dimensions, subjects per target value
df = pd.read_csv("heart.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df["target"].value_counts())

# 2. Remove duplicated patients: rows identical on all columns except bs
same_patient = df.duplicated(subset=["age", "sex", "restbps", "chol", "maxhr", "target"])
print(same_patient.sum())
df = df[same_patient == False]
print(len(df))

# 3. Data leakage: if the same patient is in both the training and the test set,
# the model is tested on subjects it has already seen (and can memorize). The
# test accuracy is then too optimistic and does not reflect new patients.

# 4. Seed (random_state) and 70/30 split
df_train, df_test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

# 5. Standardize the predictors by the mean and sd of the training set only
# Why not the test set: the test set stands for new subjects the model has never
# seen. Using its mean and sd leaks information from the test set into the model,
# and makes the evaluation too optimistic.
predictors = ["age", "sex", "restbps", "chol", "bs", "maxhr"]
train_mean = df_train[predictors].mean()
train_sd   = df_train[predictors].std()

x_train = (df_train[predictors] - train_mean) / train_sd
x_test  = (df_test[predictors] - train_mean) / train_sd
y_train = df_train["target"]
y_test  = df_test["target"]


#### THREE MODELS ####

# 1. Logistic regression: predicted probabilities for the test set
logit_model = LogisticRegression()
logit_model.fit(x_train, y_train)
logit_prob  = logit_model.predict_proba(x_test)[:, 1]
logit_class = np.where(logit_prob >= 0.5, 1, 0)

# 2. KNN with K = 15: predicted class for the test set
knn_model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15)
knn_model.fit(x_train, y_train)
knn_class = knn_model.predict(x_test)

# 3. Random forest with 500 trees: predicted probabilities and class
rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=42)
rf_model.fit(x_train, y_train)
rf_prob  = rf_model.predict_proba(x_test)[:, 1]
rf_class = np.where(rf_prob >= 0.5, 1, 0)


#### COMPARE PERFORMANCE ####

# 1. Confusion matrix for each model (rows = actual 0/1, columns = predicted 0/1)
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, logit_class))
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, knn_class))
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, rf_class))

# 2. A function that returns accuracy, sensitivity and specificity
def get_metrics(actual, predicted):
    actual = np.array(actual)
    predicted = np.array(predicted)
    accuracy    = np.mean(predicted == actual)
    sensitivity = np.sum((predicted == 1) & (actual == 1)) / np.sum(actual == 1)
    specificity = np.sum((predicted == 0) & (actual == 0)) / np.sum(actual == 0)
    return {"accuracy": accuracy, "sensitivity": sensitivity, "specificity": specificity}

# 3. One table: a row per model, a column per metric
results = pd.DataFrame(
    [get_metrics(y_test, logit_class),
     get_metrics(y_test, knn_class),
     get_metrics(y_test, rf_class)],
    index=["Logistic regression", "KNN (K = 15)", "Random forest"]
)
print(results)

# 4. Bar plot of the accuracy of the three models
plt.bar(results.index, results["accuracy"])
plt.title("Test accuracy by model")
plt.xlabel("Model")
plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
plt.show()

# 5. Which model is better?
# After removing the duplicated patients the three models are close (about 0.7
# accuracy), and with only ~90 test patients the differences are small. Logistic
# regression is the simplest and about as good as the others, so I would prefer it.
# Before deciding we would want to know the cost of each error: missing a sick
# patient (low sensitivity) is usually worse than a false alarm, so we may prefer
# the model with the best sensitivity, or lower the 0.5 threshold. We would also
# check that the differences are stable across other splits of the data (see bonus).


#### BONUS ####

# 1. AUC and ROC curves for logistic regression and random forest
print("AUC logistic:", roc_auc_score(y_test, logit_prob))
print("AUC random forest:", roc_auc_score(y_test, rf_prob))

fpr_logit, tpr_logit, _ = roc_curve(y_test, logit_prob)
fpr_rf, tpr_rf, _ = roc_curve(y_test, rf_prob)
plt.plot(fpr_logit, tpr_logit, label="Logistic regression")
plt.plot(fpr_rf, tpr_rf, label="Random forest")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="gray")
plt.title("ROC curves - test set")
plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

# 2. Repeat the whole process with 5 seeds and average the accuracy
rows = []
for seed in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    df_train, df_test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.3, random_state=seed)
    train_mean = df_train[predictors].mean()
    train_sd   = df_train[predictors].std()
    x_train = (df_train[predictors] - train_mean) / train_sd
    x_test  = (df_test[predictors] - train_mean) / train_sd
    y_train = df_train["target"]
    y_test  = df_test["target"]

    logit_model = LogisticRegression().fit(x_train, y_train)
    knn_model   = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15).fit(x_train, y_train)
    rf_model    = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=seed).fit(x_train, y_train)

    rows.append({
        "seed": seed,
        "logistic": logit_model.score(x_test, y_test),
        "knn": knn_model.score(x_test, y_test),
        "rf": rf_model.score(x_test, y_test)
    })

accuracy = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(accuracy)
print(accuracy[["logistic", "knn", "rf"]].mean())
# The accuracy of each model changes by several points from seed to seed, and so
# does the ranking of the models. One split of ~300 patients is not enough to pick
# a winner; the average over seeds is more trustworthy (logistic regression is
# slightly ahead), but the models are close.
